ranked_evidence.title: Humayun - Simple English Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
ranked_evidence.snippet: # Humayun. **Mirza Nasir al-Din Muhammad Humayun** (6 March 1508 - 27 January 1556) was the second Mughal Emperor. He ruled Afghanistan, Pakistan, and parts of northern India from 1530 to 1540. He was the son of the previous emperor, Babur. His son was Akbar, one of the most famous emperors in Mughal history. In 1534, Humayun defeated Bahadur Shah and captured Gujrat. Sher Shah meanwhile regrouped and defeated Humayun, at Chausa in 1539. In 1555, Humayun returned to India and defeated the succesor of Sher Shah, Islam Shah and regained India. Humayun was the son of Babur, the founder of the Mughal dynasty. In 1539, he was defeated by the Afghan soldier Sher Shah Suri at the Battle of Chausa, and again in 1540 at Kannauj. He regained the throne in 1555 and ruled until his death in 1556, when the Mughal Empire covered almost one million square kilometers.

ranked_evidence.title: Humayun: The Second Mughal Emperor - World History Edu
ranked_evidence.snippet: # Humayun: The Second Mughal Emperor. Humayun was the second Mughal emperor who ruled over parts of modern-day Afghanistan, Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan from 1530 to 1540 and again from 1555 until his death in 1556. Nasir al-Din Muhammad, commonly known as Humayun, was born on March 6, 1508, to Emperor Babur and his favorite wife, Maham Begum. He belonged to the Timurid dynasty and was raised in a royal environment that emphasized military training and governance. As a prince, Humayun gained experience by governing regions under Babur’s rule, but his succession to the throne in 1530 at the age of 22 was fraught with challenges. Humayun succeeded Babur on December 26, 1530, as the ruler of the Mughal territories in the Indian subcontinent. Two major rivals, Sultan Bahadur of Gujarat in the southwest and Sher Shah Suri in the east, posed serious challenges. In 1539, Humayun suffered a devastating defeat at the Battle of Chausa, where Sher Shah Suri’s forces overwhelmed the Mughals.

ranked_evidence.title: HUMAYUN — The TrishSaab Blog
ranked_evidence.snippet: He was the son of Babur, and acceded the throne in 1530. Born on 17 March 1508, Humayun’s reign was marked by significant challenges, from external threats to internal instability. He reigned for 9 years and 4 months (1530 - 1540), until he was exiled, however he did return to power for another 11 months (1555 - 1556) before his untimely death. Humayun was born in Kabul and spent his early years accompanying Babur during military campaigns. However, Babur's sudden death in 1530 left the young emperor with a vast, fragile empire to rule. During his exile, Humayun sought refuge with the Persian Empire. Despite his brief second reign, Humayun laid the groundwork for the empire's revival under his son, Akbar. His resilience in reclaiming his throne despite years of exile demonstrated his determination, though his leadership continued to face criticism for its inconsistency and reliance on external support. His resilience during exile and his ability to reclaim the throne demonstrated his determination, but his struggles highlight the fragility of early Mughal rule.

ranked_evidence.title: Humayun - Wikipedia
ranked_evidence.snippet: # Humayun. Mughal emperor from 1530 to 1540 and from 1555 to 1556. **Nasir al-Din Muhammad** (Persian: نصیرالدین محمد, 6 March 1508 – 27 January 1556), commonly known by his regnal name **Humayun** (Persian: همایون, Persian pronunciation: ), was the second Mughal emperor, who ruled much of what is now eastern Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Northern India, and Pakistan from 1530 to 1540 and again from 1555 to his death in 1556. On 26 December 1530, Humayun succeeded his father Babur to the throne of Delhi as ruler of the Mughal territories in the Indian subcontinent. Early in his reign, Humayun lost his entire empire to Sher Shah Suri but regained it 15 years later with Safavid aid. The decision of Babur to divide the territories of his empire between two of his sons was unusual in India, although it had been a common Central Asian practice since the time of Genghis Khan.

ranked_evidence.title: Humayun - Second Mughal Emperor
ranked_evidence.snippet: Humayun, second Mughal emperor who ruled India from 1530-1540 and 1555-1556, known for his turbulent reign, exile to Persia, and eventual restoration of Mughal power. Humayun lost his entire empire to Sher Shah Suri and spent 15 years in exile in Persia before dramatically reclaiming his throne. His reign was characterized by two distinct periods: his first reign from 1530 to 1540, and his restoration from 1555 until his death in 1556. Despite the brevity of his rule and the challenges he faced, Humayun's significance in Indian history lies in his role as the crucial link between the empire's founder Babur and its greatest ruler, his son Akbar. His life story is one of dramatic reversals of fortune—from inheriting an empire at age 22, to losing it completely to the Afghan leader Sher Shah Suri, to living in exile in Persia for 15 years, and finally reclaiming his throne just months before his untimely death.

ranked_evidence.title: Humāyūn | History | Research Starters | EBSCO Research
ranked_evidence.snippet: Humāyūn was the second emperor of the Mughal Empire in India, ascending to the throne at the young age of twenty-two after the death of his father, Bābur, in 1530. Born in Afghanistan, he was significantly influenced by Afghan-Turk culture and played a vital role in his father's early military victories that established Mughal dominance in North India. Despite showing considerable military talent, Humāyūn's reign was marred by personal indulgences and challenges from within his own family, particularly from his brothers, as well as external threats like the formidable Shēr Khan Sur. Humāyūn faced multiple setbacks, including a disastrous defeat at the Battle of Chausa in 1539, forcing him into exile for several years. He eventually regained the throne in 1555 with the help of Persian forces after the decline of Shēr Khan Sur's successors. Humāyūn’s reign played a crucial role in solidifying Mughal rule in India, setting the stage for the empire’s future expansion under Akbar.
